title: Sort List
description:
Given the head of a singly linked list, sort it in ascending order and return the head of the sorted list.

Aim for **O(n log n)** time. Rearrange the nodes themselves rather than copying values into an array.
hints: Quick sort and heap sort rely on random access. Which O(n log n) sort only ever needs sequential access and merging?
Merge sort: split the list in half (slow/fast pointers), sort each half recursively, merge the two sorted halves.
Cut the list at the midpoint by setting the previous node's next to None, otherwise the recursion never terminates. Reuse your Merge Two Sorted Lists routine.
approach:
**Key insight: merge sort is the natural O(n log n) sort for linked lists.** Splitting a list in half and merging two sorted lists both need only sequential access and pointer rewiring, with no random access and no extra arrays.

**Algorithm.** Base case: zero or one node is already sorted. Otherwise find the middle with slow/fast pointers (start `fast` at `head.next` so a two-node list splits 1/1), cut the list by setting `slow.next = None`, sort both halves recursively, and merge them with the standard dummy-head merge.

**Why it works.** The recursion depth is O(log n) because each level halves the list, and each level does O(n) work in splitting and merging. Correctness is the usual merge-sort argument: merging two sorted lists produces a sorted list containing all nodes.

**Common mistakes.** Forgetting to cut the list (infinite recursion). Starting `fast` at `head` so a two-node list splits 0/2 and never shrinks. Copying values into a Python list and calling `sort()`: correct and O(n log n), but O(n) extra space and not what the question tests. Quadratic insertion sort on the list.

**Interview follow-ups.** (1) Achieve O(1) extra space (beyond the output) with **bottom-up** merge sort: merge runs of length 1, 2, 4, ... iteratively, avoiding recursion. (2) Why is quick sort a poor fit for linked lists? (3) Insertion Sort List and when it is acceptable (nearly sorted input). (4) Stability: why `<=` in the merge matters.
followups: Bottom-up merge sort with O(1) space.
